She ___ to the gym every morning before work.
The simple present is used for habitual actions; with a third-person singular subject, 'goes' is correct.
Universal truths are expressed in the simple present tense.
The train ___ at 6 p.m. every day.
Scheduled timetables are expressed in the simple present tense.
'Look!' signals an action happening at the moment of speaking, so the present continuous is used.
'These days' indicates a temporary ongoing activity, which takes the present continuous.
I ___ this film twice, so I know the story well.
The present perfect is used for past experiences whose time is not specified.
She ___ in Delhi for ten years and still lives there.
An action that began in the past and continues to the present takes the present perfect.
'Since' with an unfinished time period requires the present perfect.
The present perfect continuous describes an action continuing from a point in the past to the present.
It ___ since morning, so the roads are flooded.
The present perfect continuous is used for an action continuing up to now, often with 'since' or 'for'.
They ___ to the beach last Sunday.
A finished action with a definite past time expression takes the simple past.
He ___ a letter to his father yesterday.
'Yesterday' refers to a definite past time, so the simple past is used.
She ___ her keys and could not enter the house.
A completed action in the past is expressed in the simple past.
He ___ TV when the power went off.
The past continuous describes an action in progress when another action occurred.
While I ___ dinner, the phone rang.
'While' introduces an ongoing past action, so the past continuous is required.
They ___ football when it started raining.
A plural subject in an ongoing past action takes 'were + present participle'.
By the time we reached the station, the train ___.
The earlier of two past actions is expressed in the past perfect.
I ___ my homework before my mother returned.
The action completed before another past action takes the past perfect.
He told me that he ___ the letter the previous day.
In reported speech, an earlier past action is expressed with the past perfect.
She ___ for three hours when the guests arrived.
The past perfect continuous shows an action ongoing for a duration before another past event.
She ___ in Mumbai for five years before she moved to Delhi.
An action continuing up to a point in the past takes the past perfect continuous.
I ___ him tomorrow at the office.
'Tomorrow' indicates a future action, so the simple future is used.
I think it ___ rain in the evening.
A prediction about the future uses 'will + base verb'.
This time next week, we ___ on the beach.
'This time next week' refers to an action in progress at a future time, which takes the future continuous.
When the teacher entered, the students ___ loudly.
The past continuous describes the action already in progress when another action occurred.
By 2030, the company ___ its fifth branch.
'By + future time' signals an action completed before that time, requiring the future perfect.
By next June, she ___ her degree.
The future perfect is used for an action that will be completed before a stated future time.
By next month, he ___ here for two years.
The future perfect continuous expresses the duration of an action up to a future point.
She said that she ___ busy that day.
In reported speech, the present tense of the original statement is normally shifted to the past.
He said that he ___ come the next day.
'Will' changes to 'would' when a future statement is reported in the past.
She usually ___ up at six, but today she ___ up late.
The habitual action takes the simple present ('gets'), while the completed action today takes the simple past ('woke').
I wish I ___ more time to prepare for the interview.
A wish about an unreal present situation is expressed with the past tense after 'wish'.
It is time we ___ the meeting.
After 'it is time', the past subjunctive form is used to express an overdue action.
The workers has been demanding (A)/ a revision of their wages (B)/ for the last six months (C)/ without any success. (D)/ No error (E)
The plural subject 'workers' requires 'have been demanding', not 'has been demanding'.
I am knowing (A)/ the answer (B)/ to this question (C)/ very well. (D)/ No error (E)
'Know' is a stative verb and is not normally used in the continuous form; use 'I know'.
He has completed (A)/ the assignment (B)/ yesterday (C)/ before leaving the office. (D)/ No error (E)
The present perfect cannot be used with a definite past time expression like 'yesterday'; use 'completed'.
She told me (A)/ that she has visited (B)/ the museum (C)/ the previous week. (D)/ No error (E)
In reported speech, the present perfect shifts to the past perfect: 'had visited'.
By the time she will arrive, (A)/ we will have finished (B)/ all the preparations (C)/ for the party. (D)/ No error (E)
A time clause beginning with 'by the time' takes the present tense for a future event: 'she arrives'.
Choose the sentence that uses the past tense correctly.
A) I have seen him yesterday.
C) I had seen him yesterday.
D) I am seeing him yesterday.
A definite past time expression such as 'yesterday' requires the simple past tense.
Choose the sentence that uses the present perfect continuous correctly.
A) She has been teaching here since five years.
B) She has been teaching here for five years.
C) She is teaching here since five years.
D) She teaches here since five years.
E) She has taught here since five years.
A duration takes 'for', and an action continuing to the present takes the present perfect continuous.
